content: 1. Sadeghi-Bazargani et al. (2012) conducted a case-control study to identify household-related predictors of burn injuries within an Iranian population. The study was published in BMC Public Health and provides insights into risk factors associated with burn injuries in domestic settings. 2. Stewart et al. (2016) performed a multi-center case-control study to investigate modifiable risk factors for scald injuries in children under the age of five. Published in Burns, the study highlights preventable causes of scald injuries and emphasizes the importance of targeted interventions. 3. Taira et al. (2011) explored predictors of sustaining burn injuries and assessed the effectiveness of common prevention strategies. This study, published in Journal of Burn Care & Research, examined whether the implementation of preventive measures significantly reduces the risk of burn injuries. 4. Johnston et al. (2011) conducted a pilot case-control study in the United States to examine pediatric falls from windows. The study identified cases as unintentional falls of children under 10 years of age from household windows, requiring medical evaluation. Controls were ageand gender-matched children treated for other injuries, such as burns, within two weeks of the incident. The study measured window characteristics, including type, presence of locks or guards, and sill height, to identify risk factors. Limitations included recruitment challenges and potential overmatching between cases and controls. 5. Clouatre et al. (2013) analyzed the incidence of hot tap water scalds in Ontario following the introduction of regulations. This retrospective cohort study utilized data from national healthcare databases between 2002 and 2010. The study noted a decreasing trend in scald injuries even before the intervention, suggesting potential confounding factors such as increased public awareness. The low incidence of hospitalizations limited the ability to detect statistically significant changes. 6. Phillips et al. (2011) conducted an economic evaluation alongside a randomized trial to assess the cost-effectiveness of installing thermostatic mixer valves (TMVs) in social housing in the United Kingdom. The intervention included educational materials and TMV installation to limit water temperature to 45°C. Results showed a significant reduction in severe scald injuries requiring hospitalization. However, the study faced limitations in generalizability and relied on assumptions for emergency department visit estimates. 7. Kendrick et al. (2012) performed a systematic review on home safety education and the provision of safety equipment for injury prevention. The review included 98 studies, primarily randomized controlled trials, and found evidence of improved possession and use of safety equipment. However, there was insufficient evidence to link these interventions to reductions in thermal injuries or poisoning. Free or low-cost safety equipment was more effective in promoting safety practices. 8. Turner et al. (2011) reviewed interventions modifying the home environment to reduce injuries. The review included 29 randomized trials and focused on structural modifications such as grab rails, stair gates, and fireguards. While some interventions improved safety features, there was insufficient evidence to confirm a reduction in injury rates, particularly among children and older adults. 9. McClure et al. (2005) reviewed population-based interventions aimed at preventing fall-related injuries in older adults. The review included six community trials and reported reductions in fall-related injuries ranging from 6% to 33%. However, the studies varied in methodology, and secular trends in injury rates were not fully accounted for. 10. DiGuiseppi et al. (2001) reviewed interventions promoting smoke alarm ownership and functionality. The review included 26 studies, of which 17 were randomized trials. While smoke alarm promotion programs modestly increased ownership and functionality, there was no demonstrated effect on reducing fire-related injuries or fires themselves. 11. Gates et al. (2008) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on multifactorial assessments and targeted interventions to prevent falls and injuries among older adults in community and emergency care settings. The review included 19 studies and found a reduction in fall-related injuries in some trials. However, no significant differences were observed in hospital admissions or other outcomes.
